frame: A space station log has drifted down to Twotide Atoll. The Whoshell is puzzled.
text: Captain Abena Osei had been alone on Station Kestrel for two hundred and eleven days, and she had grown used to its sounds: the hum of the air filters, the tick of the cooling pipes, the groan of metal as the station swung into sunlight. The knocking was new. It began on Tuesday, three soft taps behind the wall of the galley, then a pause, then three more. At first she blamed the pipes. By Thursday she had stopped blaming anything and started recording. 'Station log, day 212,' she said into the microphone, keeping her voice steady. 'I can hear knocking inside the walls again. Out of the box, it looks rather like a typewriter with no paper, and it plugs into the back of your television set. For readers who have never used one, the keyboard is the part with the letters on it. The Zephyr has a whopping 64 kilobytes of memory, which the makers say is 'more than any family could ever need'. The Zephyr costs about as much as a second-hand car, so most families will need to save for a while. Games are loaded from a cassette tape, and our favourite, Space Moth, took only twelve minutes to load, which is very fast indeed. While you wait, the screen flashes in rainbow stripes and the speaker makes a noise like an angry kettle. Our tester's children played Space Moth for six hours straight, and we are told that one of them has started dreaming in rainbow stripes. Some parents have written to us worrying that home computers will turn children's brains to porridge. We think that is unlikely, but we will report back next month.
